title: Integer and floating-point arithmetic
kicker: ENCT 303 · Computer Organization and Architecture · Chapter 5
subtitle: How a fixed number of bits represents negatives and fractions, and how the ALU adds, multiplies and divides them.

sections.title: Signed integers
sections.body: Sign–magnitude spends one bit on the sign (two zeros, awkward adders). 1's complement inverts all bits (still two zeros). 2's complement is universal: invert and add 1. There is one zero, addition works the same for signed and unsigned numbers, and an n-bit word covers −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹−1. To widen a number, copy the sign bit leftwards (sign extension).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: One more negative than positive value, because zero uses a non-negative pattern.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — encodings of −5
figures.note: −5 in 8 bits: sign-magnitude, 1's and 2's complement side by side (2's = 11111011).

sections.title: Addition, subtraction and overflow
sections.body: Subtraction is addition of the two’s complement: A − B = A + (¬B) + 1, so one adder does both. Overflow occurs when the true result does not fit: adding two positives gives a negative (or two negatives a positive). Hardware detects it as “carry into the sign bit ≠ carry out of the sign bit”. The carry flag is for unsigned overflow; the overflow flag is for signed.

worked.why: Two positives gave a negative pattern (−106): signed overflow.

questions.prompt: When can adding a positive and a negative number overflow?

choices.text: Whenever the carry flag is set.
Never — the result lies between the two operands.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Overflow needs operands of the same sign.

sections.title: Multiplication: shift-and-add and Booth
sections.body: Schoolbook binary multiplication adds a shifted copy of the multiplicand for each 1 in the multiplier. Booth's algorithm multiplies signed numbers directly and skips runs of 1s: it inspects pairs of multiplier bits (Q₀, Q₋₁) — 10 subtracts M, 01 adds M, 00/11 do nothing — then shifts arithmetically right. Watch 7 × (−3) with 4 bits: the answer -21 appears as 11101011.

questions.prompt: In Booth’s algorithm, the bit pair Q₀Q₋₁ = 10 means…

choices.text: Subtract the multiplicand (a run of 1s begins).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: 10 marks the start of a block of ones, handled by one subtraction instead of many additions.

problems.answer: Result -21 = 11101011 in 8 bits (two's complement of 21 is 11101011).

sections.title: Division
sections.body: Restoring division mirrors long division: shift the remainder left bringing down the next dividend bit, subtract the divisor, and if the result is negative restore (add back) and record a 0, otherwise record a 1. Non-restoring division avoids the restore step by adding instead of subtracting in the next cycle. Either takes one step per quotient bit.

worked.why: Quotient bits by repeated subtract/restore: 0011 with remainder 1.

questions.prompt: In restoring division, when is the divisor added back?

choices.text: When the subtraction gave a negative remainder.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The quotient bit is 0 and the remainder is restored.

sections.title: Floating point: IEEE 754
sections.body: A floating-point number is ±1.f × 2ᵉ stored as sign | biased exponent | fraction. Single precision uses 1 + 8 + 23 bits with bias 127; double uses 1 + 11 + 52 with bias 1023. The leading 1 is implicit. Step through 5.75: it is 101.11₂ = 1.0111 × 2², the exponent stored is 2 + 127 = 129, and the hex word is 40B80000.

questions.prompt: Why is the exponent stored with a bias?

choices.text: To save a sign bit for the mantissa.
To make it twice as precise.
So it is always non-negative and floating-point numbers compare like integers.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The sign has its own bit.

sections.title: Floating-point arithmetic
sections.body: To add: align the exponents by shifting the smaller number right, add the significands, normalise, round. To multiply: add exponents (subtract one bias), multiply significands, normalise. Division subtracts exponents. Because results are rounded, floating-point addition is not associative, and subtracting nearly equal numbers loses digits (cancellation).

questions.prompt: The first step of floating-point addition is…

choices.text: Align the exponents by shifting the smaller operand’s significand right.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Only numbers with equal exponents can have their significands added.
